reference.source: Valvular heart disease guidelines / cardiology references
clinicalPearls: Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, worldwide most often a late consequence of rheumatic fever
Presents with exertional breathlessness, fatigue, haemoptysis and, frequently, atrial fibrillation
The classic auscultatory findings are a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
Left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation and to left atrial thrombus with systemic embolism
Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure develop as the disease advances
Assessment of severity and valve morphology guides balloon valvuloplasty or surgery; anticoagulation is needed for atrial fibrillation or thrombus
reference.pathophysiology: Rheumatic mitral stenosis results from chronic post-inflammatory scarring after rheumatic fever, with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and chordal shortening progressively narrowing the mitral orifice. The obstruction raises left atrial pressure, which is transmitted back to the pulmonary circulation causing pulmonary congestion and, over time, pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain. Left atrial dilatation and stasis promote atrial fibrillation and thrombus formation with embolic risk. Although the valve injury is a sequela of infection, the established stenosis is a structural, non-infective disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Left atrial myxoma obstructing the valve
Other causes of pulmonary hypertension and breathlessness
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography with valve area and gradient and morphology scoring
Chest radiograph for left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion
Assessment for left atrial thrombus (often transoesophageal)
Right heart assessment for pulmonary hypertension
redFlags: New atrial fibrillation with rapid deterioration
Systemic embolism or left atrial thrombus
Severe pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive; symptoms and complications are well controlled and prognosis improved by timely balloon valvuloplasty or valve surgery, though atrial fibrillation and embolism carry ongoing risk.
pitfalls: Missing left atrial thrombus before valvuloplasty
Attributing breathlessness to lung disease alone
management: Relieve congestive symptoms with diuretics and control the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation with beta-blockers or other rate-limiting agents
Anticoagulate with a vitamin K antagonist for atrial fibrillation or left atrial thrombus
Refer for percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty in suitable patients with favourable valve morphology
Proceed to surgical mitral valve repair or replacement when valvuloplasty is unsuitable or the valve is heavily diseased
Continue secondary antibiotic prophylaxis against recurrent rheumatic fever
Screen for left atrial thrombus with transoesophageal echocardiography before valvuloplasty
Monitor with serial echocardiography for progression, pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain
